strand: Model input assumptions: DESNZ gas weather correction (calibration target), in-use condensing boiler efficiency, domestic hot water, indoor temperature / set point, internal gains
method_note: Every source was downloaded on 2026-11-07 (PDFs read via pdftotext; DESNZ workbooks read cell by cell). Quotes are verbatim from the extracted text; whitespace in table rows is collapsed. 'Derived' figures are the reviewer's arithmetic on the source's numbers, not the source's own claim. SAP 10.2 gains and hot-water figures for given floor areas were computed from the published equations (Table 5, Appendix J, Appendix L).

sources.harvard: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (2026) Subnational consumption statistics: methodology and guidance booklet. July 2026. London: DESNZ. Available at: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a68b45b83f71b8684d02105/Subnational-methodology-and-guidance-booklet.pdf (Accessed: 7 November 2026).

claims.claim: DESNZ sub-national gas statistics (including the domestic MSOA/LSOA series) are weather corrected; electricity is not.
claims.quote: Gas consumption figures have been weather corrected.
claims.locator: Table 1 'Key information for subnational consumption datasets', Gas row, printed p. 6

claims.claim: The correction is Xoserve's, applied to each meter's Annual Quantity (AQ), and uses regional temperature AND wind speed with trends, i.e. the gas-industry composite weather variable, not degree-days on a Met Office climate normal.
claims.quote: Xoserve adjust the AQ using a weather correction factor which accounts for regional temperature and wind speed and incorporates trends
claims.locator: Section 2.2 Methodology, 'Annualised and weather corrected MPRN-level gas consumption data', printed p. 14 (PDF p. 15)

claims.claim: An AQ is built from two meter reads 6-18 months apart, so it is a meter-level annualised, weather-normalised estimate, not a billed year.
claims.quote: An AQ is an estimate of annualised consumption using consumption recorded between two meter readings at least six months apart (with a maximum span of 18 months).
claims.locator: Section 2.1.2, 'Annual Quantity (AQ) data limitations', printed p. 13

claims.claim: Stale AQs are carried forward when no new read arrives.
claims.quote: in 2019/20 there were 2 million MPRNs that had the same AQ as 2018/19.

claims.claim: 'Domestic' is defined by consumption (AQ below 73,200 kWh), not by dwelling, so some small businesses are included.
claims.quote: DESNZ uses the gas industry standard “Annual Quantity” (AQ) cut-off point of 73,200 kWh and classifies all consumers using under that annual consumption as domestic consumers.

claims.claim: The gas 'year' is mid-May to mid-May from 2019; the latest release (December 2025) covers mid-May 2024 to mid-May 2025 (labelled '2024' in the workbooks).
claims.quote: for 2019 onwards the gas year has remained mid-May to mid-May.
claims.locator: Section 2.2 'Dates for gas period', Table 2, printed p. 15; Table 1 p. 6 gives 'mid-May 2024 to mid-May 2025' for the 2024/25 data

sources.harvard: Department of Energy and Climate Change (2014) Overview of weather correction of gas industry consumption data. Last updated 3 November 2014. London: DECC. Available at: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a7d598040f0b60a7f1a9fad/Overview_of_Weather_Correction_of_Gas_Industry_Data.pdf (Accessed: 7 November 2026).

claims.claim: The AQ is defined as consumption for a 365-day year under SEASONAL NORMAL weather (the gas industry's own normal), per End User Category and LDZ.
claims.quote: It represents an estimate of the consumption at a meter point (a single point of gas supply) for a 365-day year, under seasonal normal weather conditions.

claims.claim: The adjustment uses daily weather factors per EUC (33 EUCs x 13 LDZs) derived from a sample of over 12,000 daily-read meters; it is described as weather-desensitisation.
claims.quote: The adjustment applied to arrive at an AQ is effectively a “weather-desensitisation” rather than a correction

claims.claim: The seasonal normal basis is revised about every five years (a review was due effective October 2015).
claims.quote: The daily values of seasonal normal weather are reviewed every five years or so, with the next review due to be effective for October 2015.

sources.harvard: National Grid Gas (2020) Gas Demand Forecasting Methodology. July 2020. Warwick: National Grid. Available at: https://www.nationalgas.com/sites/default/files/documents/Gas%20Demand%20Forecasting%20Methodology%202020_v1.pdf (Accessed: 7 November 2026).

claims.claim: The seasonal normal composite weather (SNCW) is a climate-change-adjusted normal, not a raw historical average.
claims.quote: The CCM seasonal normal composite weather (SNCW) is based on historical weather adjusted for forecast warming of the UK climate.
claims.locator: Appendix A1.4 'CCM seasonal normal weather', PDF p. 29

claims.claim: The basis in force in 2020 represented the expected average climate of 2015-2020, built from weather history since October 1960 uplifted with Met Office climate increments to that period.
claims.quote: calculate predicted hourly data that represents the average climate conditions expected in 2015-2020
claims.locator: Appendix A1.4, PDF p. 29; history back to 1 October 1960 per A1.2, p. 28

claims.claim: Correcting to seasonal normal is done so that years can be compared on the same weather.
claims.quote: We do this by correcting records of actual weather to seasonal normal weather basis which is the same for all years.
claims.locator: Section 2.2 'Seasonal Normal Weather and Weather Correction', PDF p. 13

sources.harvard: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (2025) Subnational non-weather-corrected gas consumption, Great Britain, 2015-2024 [Excel workbook]; and Subnational gas consumption, Great Britain, 2005-2024 [Excel workbook, weather corrected, revised 5 May 2026]. claims.claim: DESNZ also publishes NON-weather-corrected LA/regional gas for 2015-2024 (not at MSOA level).
claims.quote: These estimates are non-weather-corrected. This means that the effect of differences in weather conditions between years has not been removed from the statistics.

claims.claim: GB mean domestic gas per meter, 2024 (mid-May 2024 to mid-May 2025): 11,359 kWh weather corrected vs 10,745 kWh actual, so the weather-corrected figure is 5.7% higher (that year was milder than seasonal normal). The ratio ranged 0.963-1.062 over 2015-2024 (derived).
claims.quote: Xoserve provide the AQs on a weather corrected basis by a process which accounts for regional temperatures and wind speed and incorporates trends.
claims.locator: Weather-corrected workbook 'Cover sheet'; numbers read from the Great Britain row of sheet '2024' in both workbooks (derived ratio)

claims.claim: Field trial of 60 condensing boilers; conclusions rest on 43 with a full year (31 combi, 10 regular, 2 CPSU).
claims.quote: The main conclusions are based on the results from 43 boilers for which a full 12 month data set has been obtained.

claims.claim: Measured annual efficiency of combi boilers (space heating + hot water, gas in): mean 82.5%, SD 4.0%; range 68.6-89.7%; SEDBUK mean 90.3%.
claims.quote: The mean efficiency2 of the trial set of combination boilers was 82.5% with a standard deviation of 4.0%.
claims.locator: Executive summary, PDF p. iv; range in field-trial combination-boiler results, PDF p. 39

claims.claim: Regular boilers: mean 85.3% (SD 2.5%) at the boiler vs SEDBUK 90.4%; with about 900 kWh/yr cylinder and primary losses the system figure is about 80.3%.
claims.quote: The mean efficiency3 of the trial set of regular boilers was 85.3% with a standard deviation of 2.5%. This is significantly less than that suggested by the mean SEDBUK seasonal efficiency of 90.4%

claims.claim: Efficiencies are on a GROSS (higher) calorific value basis, the same basis as metered gas kWh.
claims.quote: The simple “efficiency” of the boilers is calculated from heat out divided by the energy of the gas used (based on the higher calorific value) as a percentage.

claims.claim: The trial recommended an in-use correction of about 0.95 on rated seasonal efficiency.
claims.quote: SAP incorporates a ‘System correction factor’ for condensing boilers of ~0.95

claims.claim: Demand temperature: 21 C in the living area; elsewhere Th2 = 21 - 0.5 HLP (control type 1) or 21 - HLP + HLP^2/12 (types 2-3), with heating 07:00-09:00 and 16:00-23:00 on weekdays. So 'elsewhere' is not a flat 18 C; it falls with the heat-loss parameter HLP.
claims.locator: Table 9 'Heating periods and heating temperatures', footnote a, PDF p. 109 (Th1 = 21; Th2 formulas in table body)

claims.quote: Internal gains from lights, appliances, cooking and from the occupants of the dwelling (metabolic gains) are estimated from floor area (Table 5).
claims.locator: Section 5, p. 176; Table 5 p. 177; Appendix L eq. (L13); worksheet (42) for N

claims.locator: Appendix J step 6, eq. (J14) p. 82; step 3 eq. (J11); step 7 distribution loss

recommendations.calibration_target: DESNZ domestic gas is weather-corrected to the gas-industry seasonal normal (composite weather variable, temperature and wind, climate-adjusted to about 2015-2020), NOT to a 1991-2020 Met Office normal. Either (a) keep the weather-corrected MSOA target and drive the calibration with a normal-year weather series, or (b) scale the target by the non-weather-corrected/weather-corrected ratio (GB 2024: 10,745/11,359 = 0.946; regional/LA ratios are available) and drive it with actual mid-May 2024 to mid-May 2025 weather. Replace the docstring claim '1991-2020 normal weather'.
recommendations.eta: Normal(mean 0.84, sd 0.035), truncated to [0.72, 0.91], gross CV, applied to space heat plus hot water at the tap. Evidence: EST 2009 combi 82.5 +/- 4.0, regular system about 80-85; SAP default 84. Current U(0.85, 0.92), mean 0.885, sits about 4 points above the evidence.
recommendations.dhw_kWh_day: Heat delivered by the boiler = (hot-water energy at the tap) x 1.15. Tap energy = 4.18 x (46 + 26N) x 36.7/3600 kWh/day, with lognormal household scatter (sigma about 0.4). Gives a mean of about 5.3 kWh/day at N = 2.4 and a 5-95% range of about 2.5-10. Current U(2, 8) has about the right mean but the wrong shape: it misses the upper tail and is not linked to occupancy.
recommendations.tset_24h_mean: If tset is the constant 24-hour whole-house temperature (as in stock_day), use Normal(18.8, 1.0) truncated to [16, 21.5], lower by about 1 K for EPC E-G and pre-1919 homes. Use U(19, 21) or the EFUS IQR 19-21 only for a THERMOSTAT set point with intermittent heating. Current U(19, 21.5), mean 20.25, is about 1.5 K above measured 24-hour means.
recommendations.gains_W: SAP 10.2 typical gains by floor area, about 360 W (50 m2) to 630 W (120 m2), times U(0.75, 1.25). The current U(250, 700), mean 475, is consistent with a 70-90 m2 home but should scale with floor area or occupancy. The daily profile is unsourced.
